claims.claim: The 1833 Treaty of Chicago ceded about 5 million acres from the Council of Three Fires.
claims.note: Signed September 26, 1833. Terms include $14,000 a year for twenty years and $70,000 for schools, matching the deep dive stats.
claims.source: Treaty of Chicago (1833); Rooted Forward land deep dive stats (acresCeded, cashPromised, schoolsPromised)

claims.claim: The Black Hawk War of 1832 preceded and set up the cession, though the Potawatomi were not combatants.
claims.note: Band of about 1,000; roughly 150 survivors after Bad Axe, August 2, 1832. Repo verify note confirms Potawatomi non-combatant framing.
claims.source: hp-research.json land verify note; land deep dive s3

claims.claim: The Potawatomi were marched west within a few years of the treaty.
claims.note: Three-year removal clause; last annuity dance August 1835; removals through 1838.
claims.source: hp-research.json land film script (fact-checked); land deep dive s4 and s5

claims.claim: Paul Cornell bought 300 acres from Nathan Watson's widow in 1853.
claims.note: Film script names the widow purchase; the formation factcheck verified the 300 acres and 1853.
claims.source: hp-research.json land script; hp-factcheck.json formation chapter; Hyde Park Historical Society

claims.claim: About 800 men danced through Chicago at the last annuity payment in August 1835.
claims.note: Single eyewitness account by John Caton, so the fact ships at tier attributed.
claims.source: John Caton account via land deep dive stats (lastDancers)

claims.claim: In 1838 some 859 Potawatomi were force-marched 660 miles in 61 days; more than 40 died.
claims.note: Matches Trail of Death records carried in the deep dive.
claims.source: Potawatomi Trail of Death records; land deep dive s5 and stats

claims.claim: The Pokagon Band counts more than 6,000 citizens today.
claims.note: As of 2023 per the deep dive stat.
claims.source: Pokagon Band of Potawatomi; land deep dive stats (pokagonToday)

claims.claim: In 2024 the Prairie Band became the first federally recognized tribe to hold trust land in Illinois again.
claims.note: Shabbona land placed in trust.
claims.source: Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, 2024; land deep dive stats (shabbonaTrust)

claims.claim: Cornell deeded 60 acres to the Illinois Central for a 53rd Street station and six daily trains each way.
claims.note: Verified in the film factcheck.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json formation chapter; Wikipedia, Paul Cornell (lawyer)

claims.claim: The Hyde Park House hotel opened in 1857.
claims.note: The destroying fire year is contested (1877 or 1879) and stays soft per the repo verify.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json formation chapter; hp-research.json formation verify

claims.claim: Mary Todd Lincoln stayed at the Hyde Park House in summer 1865 with Robert and Tad.
claims.note: About two and a half months, a few months after the assassination.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json formation chapter; Wikipedia, Hyde Park House

claims.claim: Hyde Park Township, roughly 85,000 people, voted on June 29, 1889 to join Chicago.
claims.note: Motivated by water, sewers, and services per the film factcheck.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json formation chapter; Encyclopedia of Chicago

claims.claim: Cornell priced the sorting in, keeping the lakefront expensive and pushing industry and cheaper housing outward and southward.
claims.correction: The spec's north lakefront $7,000 versus $2,000 south lot prices are not in the corpus and were excluded; the qualitative sorting claim ships instead.
claims.note: Qualitative claim carried by the fact-checked formation deep dive s6.
claims.source: Rooted Forward formation deep dive s6

claims.claim: Township population rose from 15,716 in 1880 to about 85,000 in 1889.
claims.note: 15,716 checked against the 1880 census; 85,000 is an approximation for the annexation year.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json formation chapter; Encyclopedia of Chicago

claims.claim: The 1889 annexation added about 125 square miles and 225,000 people to Chicago.
claims.note: Citywide 1889 annexation scale, of which Hyde Park Township was part.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago, Annexation; WBEZ via deep dive stats

claims.claim: Rockefeller pledged $600,000 in May 1889, conditioned on matching gifts.
claims.note: The repo verify declines to assert the exact day of the May 1889 offer.
claims.source: Goodspeed (1925); hp-research.json university verify

claims.claim: The American Baptist Education Society raised the $400,000 match through 1889 and 1890.
claims.note: Gates and Goodspeed ran the solicitations.
claims.source: Goodspeed (1925); hp-research.json university chapter

claims.claim: Marshall Field donated the original ten-acre tract holding the main quadrangles.
claims.note: Repo verify carries this at medium confidence; Field later sold the university more land.
claims.source: hp-research.json university verify; deep dive stats (first-land)

claims.claim: The university was incorporated September 10, 1890.
claims.correction: An earlier September 18, 1890 incorporation claim conflated incorporation with the date trustees elected Harper; the repo verify fixed it to September 10.
claims.note: Founding is dated by the university to July 1, 1891, when Harper took office.
claims.source: hp-research.json university verify; University of Chicago Office of the President history

claims.claim: First classes met October 1, 1892 with 594 students and about 120 faculty, including eight former college presidents.
claims.note: Figures trace to Goodspeed and are widely repeated; coeducational from the start.
claims.source: hp-research.json university verify; Goodspeed (1925)

claims.claim: The first University of Chicago, on Douglas's donated land, closed in foreclosure in 1886.
claims.note: Film verify kept the 1856 charter framing; the deep dive stat uses 1857. The 1886 closing is consistent across both.
claims.source: hp-research.json university verify; Old University of Chicago records

claims.claim: Rockefeller gave about $35 million by 1910, including a $10 million farewell gift.
claims.note: He kept his name off campus during his giving.
claims.source: hp-research.json university verify; UChicago Library exhibit

claims.claim: Harper was elected September 18, 1890, took office July 1, 1891, and earned his Yale doctorate in his teens.
claims.correction: The earlier claim of a Yale PhD at nineteen was softened to in his teens, around age eighteen, per the repo verify.
claims.note: Elected at 34, in office at 35.
claims.source: hp-research.json university verify; Harper College Archives

claims.claim: The World's Columbian Exposition opened to the public May 1, 1893.
claims.note: Dedication was October 21, 1892.
claims.source: hp-research.json worlds-fair verify; Britannica

claims.claim: The fair ran six months, closing October 30, 1893.
claims.note: Closing ceremony canceled after Mayor Harrison's assassination.
claims.source: hp-research.json worlds-fair verify; Wikipedia

claims.claim: About 27 million admissions, roughly 21.5 million of them paid.
claims.note: The repo verify flags double counting in the 27 to 28 million totals; the paid figure is the safest precise number.
claims.source: hp-research.json worlds-fair and intro verify; Britannica

claims.claim: The Illinois Central tracks were raised onto an embankment, first ordinance May 1892, splitting off the blocks people called Hyde Park East.
claims.note: Carried by the fact-checked worlds-fair deep dive s6 with the Metra Electric National Register documentation.
claims.source: Rooted Forward worlds-fair deep dive s6 and stats (icOrdinance)

claims.claim: Chicago Day, October 9, 1893, drew 751,026 admissions.
claims.correction: The researcher's 716,881 was wrong; the repo verify corrected to about 751,026, with 761,942 in sources that add staff and exhibitors.
claims.note: A record outdoor event crowd for its time.
claims.source: hp-research.json worlds-fair verify; Wikipedia

claims.claim: The first Ferris Wheel stood 264 feet with 36 cars and more than 2,000 riders at once.
claims.note: Fifty cents a turn, same as fair admission.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Ferris Wheel (1893); worlds-fair deep dive stats (ferris)

claims.claim: The fair's medical bureau counted 32 construction deaths.
claims.note: Bureau's own tally, carried in the deep dive.
claims.source: worldsfairchicago1893.com via worlds-fair deep dive stats (deaths)

claims.claim: The Palace of Fine Arts survived on its fireproof brick substructure and reopened as the Museum of Science and Industry in 1933.
claims.note: Housed the Field Columbian Museum until 1920; Rosenwald funded the rebirth.
claims.source: hp-research.json worlds-fair verify; Wikipedia, MSI

claims.claim: 10,000 copies of The Reason Why were distributed at the fair's Haitian building.
claims.note: Ida B. Wells's protest pamphlet, with Douglass presiding at the Haiti building.
claims.source: Tennessee Historical Society account via worlds-fair deep dive stats (pamphlet)

claims.claim: Colored American Day was August 25, 1893; Douglass spoke and Dunbar read.
claims.note: Carried in the deep dive stats.
claims.source: Living History of Illinois via worlds-fair deep dive stats (coloredDay)

claims.claim: The 1893 fair drove a hotel and apartment building boom in Hyde Park, hotels east of the IC tracks, cottages west.
claims.note: Standard neighborhood history; Encyclopedia of Chicago Hyde Park entry documents the exposition boom.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago, Hyde Park

claims.claim: The Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club formed in autumn 1908 with about 350 members under attorney Francis Harper.
claims.note: The spec allowed 1908 or 1909; the repo verified 1908 in both the film script and the deep dive, sourced to Spear.
claims.source: Allan Spear, Black Chicago; hp-research.json color-line film script; color-line deep dive s1

claims.claim: Chicago's Black population in 1910 was about 44,000, roughly 2 percent of the city.
claims.correction: The film said about 40,000; the repo factcheck flagged it imprecise and set about 44,000 (census 44,103). The correction is authoritative and ships.
claims.note: Encyclopedia of Chicago uses 44,000.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json color-line chapter; 1910 U.S. Census

claims.claim: By 1940 Chicago's Black population was about 278,000.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json color-line chapter; 1940 U.S. Census

claims.claim: Black Belt apartments were carved into tiny kitchenettes at exploitative rents.
claims.note: Qualitative claim per Drake and Cayton and the fact-checked deep dive.
claims.source: Black Metropolis (1945); color-line deep dive s3

claims.claim: In one day in summer 1917 the Chicago Urban League counted 664 applicants for houses with only fifty available.
claims.note: Verified against the primary text of the 1922 commission report. An appendix summary in the same report gives fifty-five dwellings; the housing chapter's figure of fifty ships.
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, The Negro in Chicago (1922), Gutenberg etext 57343

claims.claim: A late-1930s CHA study found 45 percent of kitchenette tenants paying over 30 percent of income for rent.
claims.note: Carried in the fact-checked deep dive stats.
claims.source: Chicago Housing Authority study via color-line deep dive stats (rent)

claims.claim: Chicago Defender circulation passed 125,000 by 1918 as it drove the Great Migration.
claims.note: Great Northern Drive called for spring 1917.
claims.source: color-line deep dive s2 and stats (defender)

claims.claim: The line the 1908 club drew held for about forty years, until 1948.
claims.note: Spear's framing, carried in the deep dive.
claims.source: Allan Spear, Black Chicago; color-line deep dive stats (fortyYears)

claims.claim: 58 bombings of Black homes and of real estate men's properties, July 1, 1917 to March 1, 1921.
claims.note: Verified verbatim against the 1922 report's primary text.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922), Bombings section

claims.claim: 32 of the 58 bombs exploded within the square bounded by 41st and 60th Streets, Cottage Grove Avenue and State Street.
claims.note: Verbatim from the report. The square borders Hyde Park and Kenwood.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922), Bombings section

claims.claim: Two people were killed by the bombs, both Black.
claims.note: Report also notes injuries to white and Black residents and over $100,000 in damage.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922), Bombings section

claims.claim: No one was convicted; only two suspects were ever arrested and neither was tried.
claims.note: One suspect released on $500 bond with no trial a year later, the other released after two days.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922), Bombings section

claims.claim: The pace averaged one race bombing every twenty days for three years and eight months.
claims.note: Report's own arithmetic; the deep dive carries the same pace.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922); color-line deep dive stats (bombings)

claims.claim: Property damage from the bombings exceeded $100,000 in period dollars.
claims.note: As stated by the commission.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922), Bombings section

claims.claim: The 1919 riot killed 38, twenty-three Black and fifteen white, with 537 injured.
claims.note: Matches the report's introduction and the deep dive.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922); color-line deep dive s4

claims.claim: About 1,000 people were left homeless by the riot.
claims.note: Report's casualty summary; the deep dive phrases it as about a thousand Black families burned out.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922); color-line deep dive s4

claims.claim: Jesse Binga's home and offices were bombed at least five times between 1917 and 1921.
claims.note: The commission report devotes a case study to the Binga bombings; Hayner's biography supplies the at-least-five count carried in the corpus.
claims.source: Don Hayner, Binga (2019); The Negro in Chicago (1922)

claims.claim: Eugene Williams, seventeen, drowned July 27, 1919 after drifting past the color line in the water and being struck amid stone throwing; police refused the named arrest.
claims.note: Verified against the report's riot narrative.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago (1922), riot narrative

claims.claim: The 1922 commission report runs 672 pages.
claims.note: The Negro in Chicago, University of Chicago Press, 1922; xxiv + 672 pages.
claims.source: CCRR 1922, Internet Archive scan

claims.claim: Two arrests were made across the 58 recorded bombings of 1917 to 1921.
claims.note: Verbatim in the CCRR aggregate passage alongside the zero convictions.
claims.source: The Negro in Chicago, 1922

claims.claim: After Corrigan v. Buckley (1926) racial covenants proliferated, sweeping the neighborhoods around the Black Belt from the late 1920s.
claims.note: Decision date May 24, 1926 from the court record; the covenant wave timing is in the fact-checked corpus and Covenants Project research.
claims.source: Corrigan v. Buckley, 271 U.S. 323; Chicago Covenants Project; color-line deep dive s6

claims.claim: The University of Chicago paid $83,597.46 in subsidies to neighborhood associations defending covenants, 1933 to 1947.
claims.note: Precise figure per Hirsch as specified; the corpus independently carries more than $83,000 within a more than $110,000 community interests budget over the same years.
claims.source: Hirsch, Making the Second Ghetto, covenant subsidy accounting; corroborated by color-line deep dive s6

claims.claim: Nathan MacChesney, NAREB general counsel, drafted the 1927 model covenant that real estate boards distributed across the country.
claims.note: NAREB role and 1927 drafting confirmed via the Chicago Covenants Project and Chicago Magazine; the corpus carries the 1927 model covenant callout.
claims.source: Chicago Covenants Project history; Chicago Magazine (June 2012); color-line deep dive s6

claims.claim: By the 1940s hundreds of Cook County subdivisions carried racial covenants.
claims.correction: The commonly cited claims that half, or 80 percent, of Chicago's residential land was covenanted could not be attributed to a verifiable named source and were not shipped. The corpus wording, hundreds of subdivisions, ships instead.
claims.note: The Chicago Covenants Project's mapped record supports the shipped version.
claims.source: Chicago Covenants Project; color-line deep dive s6

claims.claim: The Washington Park covenant required signatures from owners of 95 percent of frontage; only about 54 percent had signed.
claims.note: From the Hansberry v. Lee record, carried in the redlining deep dive.
claims.source: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32; redlining deep dive stats (frontage)

claims.claim: The Chicago Defender called the covenants the University of Chicago Agreement to get rid of Negroes.
claims.note: Phrase carried in the fact-checked deep dive and covenant scholarship.
claims.source: Chicago Defender via color-line deep dive s6

claims.claim: A 1928 Hyde Park Herald piece praised covenants as a marvelous delicately woven chain of armor.
claims.note: Quoted verbatim in Coates 2014, widely reproduced in covenant scholarship.
claims.source: Coates, The Case for Reparations, The Atlantic, 2014

claims.claim: In 1921 the Chicago Real Estate Board voted immediate expulsion for any member selling to a Black buyer on an all-white block.
claims.note: Unanimous vote dated May 4, 1921 in the EJI record; consistent with Hirsch and Satter.
claims.source: EJI calendar, May 4, 1921; Hirsch; Satter

claims.claim: NAREB's 1924 Code of Ethics, Article 34, barred Realtors from introducing members of any race or nationality detrimental to property values.
claims.note: Article text confirmed against archived code reproductions.
claims.source: NAREB Code of Ethics (1924); Oregon History Project records; Seattle Journal for Social Justice

claims.claim: The explicit race and nationality language was removed from the code in 1950.
claims.note: The clause stood from 1924 to 1950; vaguer wording followed.
claims.source: NAREB code revision history; Home Ownership Matters, Illinois fair housing history

claims.claim: NAR formally apologized in November 2020, through president Charlie Oppler at its fair housing summit.
claims.note: First formal apology by the association; coverage dates the remarks November 19, 2020.
claims.source: RISMedia (Nov 19, 2020); The Seattle Times; The Real Deal

claims.claim: Hoyt's 1933 One Hundred Years of Land Values in Chicago ranked races and nationalities by their supposed effect on land values, with Negroes then Mexicans at the bottom.
claims.note: Carried in the fact-checked redlining deep dive and film script.
claims.source: Homer Hoyt (1933); redlining deep dive s1; hp-research.json redlining script

claims.claim: Hoyt served as the FHA's chief land economist from 1934 to 1940.
claims.correction: The spec used principal housing economist. Both titles circulate for the same post; the repo's fact-checked film and deep dive use chief land economist, so the corpus wording ships with the variant noted.
claims.note: Either title, the author of the racial land-value hierarchy wrote federal lending economics.
claims.source: hp-research.json redlining script; redlining deep dive stats (fhaCreated); Hoyt biographies

claims.claim: The FHA Underwriting Manual, built under Frederick Babcock, told appraisers to check for incompatible racial groups and rewarded restrictive deed clauses.
claims.correction: The spec's inharmonious racial groups wording was adjusted to the corpus-verified incompatible racial groups phrasing of the 1938 edition.
claims.note: The manual also praised barriers giving protection from adverse influences.
claims.source: FHA Underwriting Manual (1938) via redlining deep dive s3

claims.claim: On the Chicago HOLC residential security map the Black Belt was washed in red, with Black presence graded as hazard.
claims.correction: The spec's claim that every Black neighborhood drew a D or C in a 1939-40 survey was softened to the corpus wording. The repo paper dates its Chicago map to 1938 and the deep dive dates the national survey 1935 to 1940.
claims.note: Area description sheets recorded race next to sewer access as the same kind of fact.
claims.source: Mapping Inequality; redlining deep dive s4; repo HOLC paper

claims.claim: Congress created the FHA in 1934 under the National Housing Act.
claims.note: Carried across the corpus.
claims.source: National Housing Act of 1934; redlining deep dive s2

claims.claim: HOLC graded 239 cities block by block, 1935 to 1940.
claims.note: A green through D red.
claims.source: HOLC City Survey via redlining deep dive stats (holcCities)

claims.claim: Under 2 percent of federally insured home loans went to Black Americans between 1945 and 1959.
claims.note: Figure carried in the fact-checked deep dive; tier reported since it rides on secondary scholarship.
claims.source: redlining deep dive s3 and stats (blackLoans)

claims.claim: Illinois created its first formal covenant-language removal process in 2022.
claims.note: Public Act 102-0110.
claims.source: Illinois Public Act 102-0110; redlining deep dive s7

claims.claim: New Deal agencies refinanced about one million home mortgages through the HOLC.
claims.note: HOLC program totals 1933-1936, just over one million loans.
claims.source: HOLC program records

claims.claim: Buchanan v. Warley, 245 U.S. 60, decided November 5, 1917, struck down racial zoning ordinances.
claims.note: Public court record. Consequence, segregation shifted to private covenants.
claims.source: Buchanan v. Warley, 245 U.S. 60 (1917)

claims.claim: Corrigan v. Buckley, 271 U.S. 323, decided May 24, 1926, dismissed the constitutional challenge to a private covenant.
claims.note: Public court record. Consequence, covenants proliferated.
claims.source: Corrigan v. Buckley, 271 U.S. 323 (1926)

claims.claim: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32, decided November 12, 1940, was won on procedural due process grounds and left covenants standing.
claims.note: Matches the repo color-line verify, which stresses the case did not reach the merits.
claims.source: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940); hp-research.json color-line verify

claims.claim: Shelley v. Kraemer, 334 U.S. 1, decided May 3, 1948, 6 to 0, barred judicial enforcement of racial covenants; the clauses remained in deeds.
claims.note: Vinson wrote; Jackson, Reed, and Rutledge recused. Verified in the film factcheck.
claims.source: Shelley v. Kraemer, 334 U.S. 1 (1948); hp-factcheck.json color-line chapter

claims.claim: The University of Chicago organized the South East Chicago Commission in 1952.
claims.correction: An earlier established in May 1952 claim was removed by the repo verify; the documented public establishment meeting was March 27, 1952, so the year ships without a month.
claims.note: Kimpton later said the university used a sensational March 1952 crime to organize it.
claims.source: hp-research.json urban-renewal verify; CEGU (2023)

claims.claim: Kimpton chaired the SECC; Julian Levi was executive director and ran it to 1980.
claims.note: Some sources misname the chancellor as Hutchins; Kimpton is correct per the repo verify.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; NYT Levi obituary (1996)

claims.claim: The renewal plan covered 856 acres.
claims.note: Verified in the film factcheck.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; UChicago Library, Renewal and Revival

claims.claim: The plan marked 638 buildings for demolition.
claims.note: Verified in the film factcheck.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; Hyde Park Herald, Lost Hyde Park

claims.claim: About 4,000 families were displaced over the program's full course.
claims.correction: The film's phrasing that 4,000 were already pushed out by 1958 was fixed by the repo factcheck; 4,000 is the full-course total. The spec's more precise 4,371 households via Rossi and Dentler was not independently verified and ships only as a note.
claims.note: Rounded figure is consistent across the NYT obit, Chicago Magazine, and AAIHS.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; Rossi and Dentler (1961)

claims.claim: The first building fell May 10, 1955, before the plan was approved.
claims.note: CEGU timeline entry verified in the film factcheck.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; CEGU (2023)

claims.claim: The City Council approved the plan November 7, 1958.
claims.note: Date verified across the corpus.
claims.source: hp-research.json intro and urban-renewal verify; UChicago Library

claims.claim: The university committed about $29 million of its own money.
claims.note: Kimpton's own figure, quoted by CEGU and verified in the film factcheck.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; CEGU (2023)

claims.claim: 46.1 percent of displaced white families relocated within Hyde Park-Kenwood in the Hyde Park A and B projects.
claims.note: Scope limited to Hyde Park A and B per the repo verify; do not generalize to the full plan.
claims.source: CEGU (2023); hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter

claims.claim: 16.6 percent of displaced Black families relocated within Hyde Park-Kenwood in those projects.
claims.note: The film voiced seventeen percent; the exact CEGU figure is 16.6.
claims.source: CEGU (2023); hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter

claims.claim: The neighborhood's Black population fell about 40 percent across the renewal.
claims.note: Verified in the film factcheck at medium confidence.
claims.source: hp-factcheck.json urban-renewal chapter; Wikipedia, Hyde Park, Chicago

claims.claim: More than 15,000 residents were displaced.
claims.note: The figure the university's own sources use, verified for the film's cold open; Chicago Magazine cites 30,000 for the broader area, so 15,000 is not a ceiling.
claims.source: hp-research.json intro verify; UChicago Library exhibit

claims.claim: Section 112 of the 1959 housing legislation let university spending count as the local urban renewal match; the university sponsored its drafting and Levi lobbied for it.
claims.note: The repo verify softened claims that Levi personally wrote the statute.
claims.source: hp-research.json urban-renewal verify; CEGU (2023); Leventhal Map Center

claims.claim: Woodlawn organizing won a 1964 commitment that the university would not expand south of 61st Street.
claims.note: Carried in the repo verify notes and deep dive stats.
claims.source: hp-research.json urban-renewal verify notes; urban-renewal deep dive stats (line61)

claims.claim: About $250 million in private investment was drawn in alongside the university's money.
claims.note: CEGU analysis figure carried in the deep dive stats.
claims.source: CEGU (2023) via urban-renewal deep dive stats (private)

claims.claim: Kimpton described renewal as a way of cutting down the number of Negroes in the neighborhood.
claims.note: Quoted by Chicago Magazine and noted in the repo intro verify; present it as an attributed quotation.
claims.source: Chicago Magazine (Jan 2018); hp-research.json intro verify notes

claims.claim: The University of Chicago abolished varsity football in December 1939.
claims.note: Board action December 21, 1939 under Hutchins.
claims.source: University of Chicago histories

claims.claim: Of 241 white-run Cook County savings and loans, exactly one would lend to Black buyers.
claims.note: Satter's figure, pp. 44-45, confirmed against published summaries of Family Properties.
claims.source: Beryl Satter, Family Properties (2009), pp. 44-45

claims.claim: Clyde Ross bought his North Lawndale home on contract for $27,500.
claims.note: The seller kept the deed until the final payment.
claims.source: Ta-Nehisi Coates, The Case for Reparations, The Atlantic (2014)

claims.claim: The speculator who sold to Ross had bought the house for $12,000 six months earlier.
claims.note: Per Coates.
claims.source: Ta-Nehisi Coates, The Case for Reparations (2014)

claims.claim: Contract buyers paid an average of $71,000 more per home than with a conventional mortgage, adjusted for inflation.
claims.note: Study figure as reported in launch coverage.
claims.source: Duke Cook Center, The Plunder of Black Wealth in Chicago (2019); Chicago Sun-Times (May 30, 2019)

claims.claim: 75 to 95 percent of homes sold to Black families in the 1950s and 60s were sold on contract.
claims.correction: The spec's single 82 percent figure was replaced with the study's published 75 to 95 percent range.
claims.note: Range carried in the fact-checked corpus and the study.
claims.source: Duke Cook Center (2019); present deep dive s5

claims.claim: The average contract buyer paid $587 more per month, in 2019 dollars, than a conventional mortgage would have cost.
claims.note: Ships as the monthly-cost framing in place of the unverified FHA-versus-contract terms comparison.
claims.source: Duke Cook Center (2019); WBEZ (May 30, 2019)

claims.claim: The average contract markup was 84 percent.
claims.note: Study figure, carried in the corpus.
claims.source: Duke Cook Center (2019); present deep dive stats (contract)

claims.claim: Contract selling stripped $3.2 to $4.0 billion from Black Chicago, in 2019 dollars.
claims.note: The film voices three to four billion; the study's published range is 3.2 to 4.0.
claims.source: Duke Cook Center (2019); hp-research.json present script

claims.claim: About 60,100 Chicago homes were bought by Black families on contract in the period.
claims.note: Study count as reported in launch coverage.
claims.source: Duke Cook Center (2019); WBEZ (May 30, 2019)

claims.claim: FHA-versus-contract monthly terms comparison, a $15,000 home at $110 a month over 25 years against a $27,000 contract at $252 a month.
claims.note: Not sourceable in this pass and NOT included in facts.json. The Duke $587 per month framing (contracts.extra_monthly_587) is the shipping alternative.

claims.claim: The Contract Buyers League formed in 1968 out of meetings in the Presentation Catholic Church basement in North Lawndale, with organizing help from Jack Macnamara.
claims.note: First community meeting January 1968; Macnamara was a Jesuit seminarian working from Msgr. Egan's parish.
claims.source: Satter, Family Properties; Coates (2014); The Chicago Reporter

claims.claim: More than 500 families joined the payment strike.
claims.note: Consistent between the Chicago Reporter account and the fact-checked corpus.
claims.source: The Chicago Reporter; present deep dive stats (league)

claims.claim: 155 contracts had been renegotiated by July 1971.
claims.correction: The spec's more than 400 matches a Wikipedia line flagged citation needed, and the corpus line of more than 450 families could not be confirmed at its cited source. The verifiable named-source count, 155 by July 1971, ships as a floor.
claims.note: Renegotiations continued after July 1971; treat the shipped number as a dated floor rather than a lifetime total. Re-tiered reported at integration. The Chicago Reporter is a published investigative outlet; the attributed tier is reserved for single-source oral claims. Corroboration against Satter, Family Properties page cites remains open.
claims.source: The Chicago Reporter, Inside the Contract Buyers League's fight against housing discrimination

claims.claim: Approximately seventy families permanently lost their homes in the strike.
